title: How to read a sakhi
hookLine: a sakhi is not a news report; it carries truth in the shape of a story

cards: Did it really happen? That's the question a lot of us carry into an old story, the way we'd carry it into a headline. Who saw it?
Where's the proof? This week we've met the janamsakhis: the old telling, the friend's telling, Miharban's telling, the painted pages.
Soon they'll hand us oil that goes cool, bitter fruit made sweet, and a land of enchantment. So first, a tool for the road. Today: sakhi.

teach.b: A sakhi is a story of the Guru's life, told and retold by the people who loved him. It isn't a news report. It carries truth in the shape of a story.
So the first question to ask it isn't did this happen. It's what does it know. Take one we met in the Puratan telling.
Nanak, a grown man working at the storehouse, goes down to the river near Sultanpur to bathe, and doesn't come back. His friends search the banks.
Tradition says that after days he returns, sits in silence, and when he finally speaks, his first words are: there is no Hindu, and there is no Musalman. Read it with three questions.

teach.h: WHAT HAPPENS, WHAT THE BANI SAYS.
teach.b: What happens? A man goes under the water and comes up changed. What does the Guru's own word say?
Set the sakhi beside the Guru Granth Sahib, which opens with One: one Creator. Some readers hear in that One something deeper than the names people fight over. What does the story know?
That this teaching came from somewhere deeper than a debate: out of the river, out of an encounter, with a message for both of Nanak's neighbors at once. Sikhs hold the sakhis in more than one way.
Some take the wonders just as they're told; others read them as pictures of a truth too big for plain sentences. Both can ask the same question.
And a test keeps a sakhi honest: if a story seems to teach something the Guru's own hymns would never say, Sikh teachers say the hymns win.
The sakhi is the lamp you carry to it.

how: Sikh teachers and kathakars tell sakhis of Guru Nanak's life to draw out a teaching, and they treat the Guru Granth Sahib as the measure any sakhi must agree with.

one story of the Guru's life, told to teach

games.q: a friend reads the river sakhi and asks you, flatly: did that really happen? you want to read it the way today's lesson suggests. what do you ask first?
o: who was there with a camera?
games.why: a sakhi carries truth in the shape of a story. ask what it knows first, and check it against the Guru's own word. readers who take the wonder literally and readers who don't can both answer that.

practice: Pick one sakhi we've met this year, milk and jasmine at Multan, the true bargain, the river, and let the scene play once.

Then set aside whether and ask only what: what does this story know about God, about people, about how to live? Let the answer come in one short sentence, plain enough to tell a child, and if you pray, say Waheguru when it arrives.
